newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel rebuffs EU plea to ease up on Palestinians.
newsitem.headline: Israel rebuffs EU plea to ease up on Palestinians.

text.p: Israel on Monday stuck to its tough stance toward Palestinians amid a flurry of diplomacy aimed at rescuing the peace process, thrown into deep crisis by the suicide bombings in a Jerusalem market.

The European Union's Middle East envoy, Miguel Angel Moratinos, said at a Gaza news conference with Palestinian President Yasser Arafat: "We cannot really understand some measures that instead of bringing security are bringing insecurity."
He said he would try to persuade Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to lift measures imposed on Palestinians after Wednesday's bombing that killed 13 people and wounded 170.
But Netanyahu, who on Sunday put the world on notice that Israel's peacemaking with the PLO begun in 1993 might be nearing the end of the road, refused to stand down.

"Envoy Moratinos...brought a Palestinian request to ease the pressure on the Palestinan Authority and the steps Israel has taken against it," Netanyahu's office said in a statement issued after he met Moratinos later on Monday.

"The prime minister told Moratinos that Israel was acting against terror and not against the Palestinian people...and that Israel was taking different steps in order to pressure the Palestinian Authority to fulfil its obligations."

Netanyahu's government suspended peace talks with the PLO in reaction to Wednesday's attack and sealed off the West Bank and Gaza Strip, preventing tens of thousands of Palestinians from reaching their jobs in the Jewish state.
It also threatened to enter Palestinian self-rule areas to fight militants if Arafat did not do the job. Israel has arrested 145 suspected militants in areas under its control.
U.S. peace envoy Dennis Ross is expected to visit the region later this week. Netanyahu was quoted by his office as saying:
"I think it is acceptable that Dennis Ross deal mainly with the security issue. Perhaps not mainly, but only, the security issue on this trip."
Earlier, Netanyahu had said the Authority had to decide to be "a regime that fights terrorism like Jordan and Egypt, or a regime that encourages terrorism like Iraq and Iran".
He made the comment before talks with U.S. Republican Senator Phil Gramm, a staunch supporter of Israel. Gramm said Congress might not renew aid to the Palestinian Authority.

"Authorisation for Palestinian aid, as you know, expires on August 12. It will not be renewed by the United States Congress in my opinion unless the Palestinians begin living up to the commitments they've made," Gramm said.

Palestinians, who suspended security cooperation with Israel after Netanyahu launched a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem in March, say they have nonetheless worked to foil attacks by militants opposed to the peace process.
A leaflet issued in the name of the Islamist Hamas group claimed responsibility for Wednesday's attack, but Israeli and Palestinian officials say they are not sure of its authenticity.
Arafat spokesman Ahmed Tibi said that in light of doubts over the bombers' identities, Netanyahu owed Arafat an apology.
"Mr Benjamin Netanyahu will do well to phone the chairman and apologise," he told Israel Radio.
On Sunday, Netanyahu told his cabinet Israel would not honour signed peace deals if Arafat did not crack down.

Arafat was to meet King Hussein later on Monday in Amman. Jordanian officials privately expressed their support of the Palestinian leader's view that the bombings were being exploited by Israel to backtrack on peace commitments.

Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy, who goes to Egypt for talks with President Hosni Mubarak on the crisis on Tuesday, said Israel "doesn't want the collapse of the Authority" but that it had to fight militants.

Israel on Monday demolished three illegally built homes in Arab East Jerusalem. Palestinians say demolitions are aimed at squeezing them out of the city. Israeli Mayor Ehud Olmert calls illegal Arab building a "cancer". Israel occupied East Jerusalem in 1967 and vows never to cede an inch of it. Palestinians want it as capital of a future state.

In south Lebanon, the last active Israeli-Arab front, Israeli commandos raided suspected pro-Iranian Hizbollah targets. Hizbollah said five guerrillas were killed by roadside bombs after the clashes. Five civilians were wounded.
